items.title: 8.2.2 Some Deductions from the binomial expansion of (a + x)^n

source_refs.note: Book p. 155-156: 8.2.2 Some Deductions from the binomial expansion of (a + x)^n, deductions (i)-(iv), sum of coefficients 2^n, odd/even coefficient sums, Example 14

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: (A) is true for every value of \(a\) and \(x\). So we may put particular values in it, such as \(a = 1\) or \(x = -1\). Each choice gives a new, useful result. These results are called deductions (consequences) of the binomial theorem.

(i) If we put \(a = 1\), in (I), then we have;
\[(1 + x)^{n} = \binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1}x + \binom{n}{2}x^{2} + \dots\]
\[+ \binom{n}{r}x^{r} + \dots + \binom{n}{n-1}x^{n-1}\]
\[+ \binom{n}{n}x^{n} \quad \text{(B)}\]
\[= 1 + nx + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{2} + \dots\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}x^{r}\]
\[+ \dots + nx^{n-1} + x^{n}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In deductions (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) the book says "in (I)", but the expansion it refers to is labelled (A). Read every "(I)" on this page as (A).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does \((n-r)!\) cancel? \(n!\) is \(n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1\). Stop the product after \(r\) factors, at \((n - r + 1)\); what is left, \((n-r)(n-r-1)\cdots 1\), is exactly \((n-r)!\), and it cancels with the denominator. So \(\binom{n}{r}\) is "\(r\) factors counting down from \(n\), divided by \(r!\)". Example: \(\binom{7}{3} = \dfrac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5}{3!} = 35\).
This second form will be important in 8.3, where \(n\) need not be a positive integer.

(ii) Putting \(a = 1\) and replacing \(x\) by \(-x\), in (I), we get
\[(1 - x)^{n} = \binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1}(-x) + \binom{n}{2}(-x)^{2}\]
\[+ \binom{n}{3}(-x)^{3} + \dots + \binom{n}{n-1}(-x)^{n-1}\]
\[+ \binom{n}{n}(-x)^{n}\]
\[= \binom{n}{0} - \binom{n}{1}x + \binom{n}{2}x^{2} - \binom{n}{3}x^{3} + \dots\]
\[+ (-1)^{n-1}\binom{n}{n-1}x^{n-1}\]
\[+ (-1)^{n}\binom{n}{n}x^{n} \quad \text{(C)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In \((1 - x)^{n}\) the terms with odd powers of \(x\) are negative and those with even powers are positive, because \((-x)^{r} = (-1)^{r}x^{r}\).

(iii) We can find the sum of the binomial coefficients by putting \(a = 1\) and \(x = 1\) in (I).
i.e.,
\[(1 + 1)^{n} = \binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{2} + \dots\]
\[+ \binom{n}{n-1} + \binom{n}{n}\]
or
\[2^{n} = \binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{2} + \dots\]
\[+ \binom{n}{n-1} + \binom{n}{n}\]
Thus, the sum of coefficients in the binomial expansion equals to \(2^{n}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check with \(n = 4\): \(1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16 = 2^{4}\).
A counting meaning: a set of \(n\) objects has \(\binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1} + \dots + \binom{n}{n}\) subsets in all (choose 0 objects, 1 object, ..., all \(n\)). Each object is either in or out, so there are \(2^{n}\) subsets. Both counts must agree.

(iv) Putting \(a = 1\) and \(x = -1\), in (I), we have
\[(1 - 1)^{n} = \binom{n}{0} - \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{2} - \binom{n}{3} + \dots\]
\[+ (-1)^{n-1}\binom{n}{n-1} + (-1)^{n}\binom{n}{n}\]
Thus
\[\binom{n}{0} - \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{2} - \binom{n}{3} + \dots\]
\[+ (-1)^{n-1}\binom{n}{n-1} + (-1)^{n}\binom{n}{n} = 0\]

If \(n\) is odd positive integer, then
\[\binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{2} + \dots + \binom{n}{n-1}\]
\[= \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{3} + \dots + \binom{n}{n}\]
If \(n\) is even positive integer, then
\[\binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{2} + \dots + \binom{n}{n}\]
\[= \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{3} + \dots + \binom{n}{n-1}\]
Thus, sum of odd coefficients of a binomial expansion equals to the sum of its even coefficients.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here "odd coefficients" means the coefficients in the odd places (1st, 3rd, 5th, ...), i.e. \(\binom{n}{0}, \binom{n}{2}, \binom{n}{4}, \dots\), and "even coefficients" those in the even places, \(\binom{n}{1}, \binom{n}{3}, \dots\). In the alternating sum the first group has \(+\) signs and the second group \(-\) signs; the total is 0, so the two groups are equal.
Since together they make \(2^{n}\) (deduction iii), each group adds up to \(2^{n-1}\). Check with \(n = 5\): \(1 + 10 + 5 = 16\) and \(5 + 10 + 1 = 16 = 2^{4}\).

blocks.title: Example 14
steps:
Given: the sum \(\binom{n}{1} + 2\binom{n}{2} + 3\binom{n}{3} + \dots + n\binom{n}{n}\).
To prove: it equals \(n \cdot 2^{n-1}\).
Method: write each \(\binom{n}{r}\) in the product form \(\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}\), cancel the multiplier \(r\) with \(r!\), take \(n\) common, and recognise the bracket as the sum of all the coefficients of \((1 + x)^{n-1}\), which is \(2^{n-1}\) by deduction (iii).

Step 1: Write the terms in product form
\[\binom{n}{1} + 2\binom{n}{2} + 3\binom{n}{3} + \dots + n\binom{n}{n}\]
\[= n + 2\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!} + 3\dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}\]
\[+ \dots + n \cdot 1\]
Why: \(\binom{n}{1} = n\), \(\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}\), \(\binom{n}{3} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}\), and \(\binom{n}{n} = 1\).

Step 2: Cancel and take \(n\) common
\[= n\left[1 + (n-1) + \dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2!} + \dots + 1\right]\]
Why: \(\frac{2}{2!} = 1\) and \(\frac{3}{3!} = \frac{1}{2!}\); in general \(\frac{r}{r!} = \frac{1}{(r-1)!}\). Every term contains the factor \(n\), so it is taken outside.

Step 3: Recognise the bracket
\[= n\left[\binom{n-1}{0} + \binom{n-1}{1} + \binom{n-1}{2} + \dots + \binom{n-1}{n-1}\right]\]
Why: \(1 = \binom{n-1}{0}\), \(n - 1 = \binom{n-1}{1}\), \(\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2!} = \binom{n-1}{2}\), ..., and the last 1 is \(\binom{n-1}{n-1}\). These are all the binomial coefficients of index \(n - 1\).

Step 4: Use deduction (iii)
\[= n \cdot 2^{n-1}\]
Why: the sum of all the binomial coefficients of index \(m\) is \(2^{m}\); here \(m = n - 1\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(a = 1\): \((1 + x)^{n} = \sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}x^{r}\), with \(\binom{n}{r} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}\).
2. \(a = 1\), \(x \to -x\): \((1 - x)^{n}\) has alternating signs.
3. \(\binom{n}{0} + \binom{n}{1} + \dots + \binom{n}{n} = 2^{n}\).
4. \(\binom{n}{0} - \binom{n}{1} + \binom{n}{2} - \dots = 0\); the sums of the coefficients in odd and in even places are equal, each \(2^{n-1}\).
5. Useful identity: \(r\binom{n}{r} = n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the sum of coefficients as \(2n\) instead of \(2^{n}\).
2. Starting the alternating sum with a minus sign: it starts \(+\binom{n}{0}\).
3. In Example 14, cancelling \(r\) with \(r!\) incorrectly: \(\frac{r}{r!} = \frac{1}{(r-1)!}\), not \(\frac{1}{r}\).
